title: Joan of Arc
hookLine: a teenage peasant hears voices, leads an army, is burned at nineteen, and is declared innocent too late
tomorrow: Camp 2 close: the story you're in

cards: Think of yourself at thirteen: your worries, what you thought you could do. Now, a village called Domrémy, in eastern France, around the year 1425.
France has been at war with England for generations, and much of the north is occupied. A peasant girl named Jeanne, Joan, can't read or write. She spins wool and helps in the fields.
She says that in her father's garden she began to hear voices, which she came to know as Saint Michael, Saint Catherine and Saint Margaret. They tell her to be good and go to church.
Over the next few years, they tell her something impossible: go to the king's heir, and help drive the English out.

teach.b: At seventeen, Joan talks her way past soldiers and nobles to Charles, the uncrowned heir, and somehow convinces him.

She's given armor and a banner, and in the spring of 1429 she rides with the army to the besieged city of Orléans. Within days the siege is broken. That summer she stands beside Charles as he's crowned king at Reims.
A year later she's captured, sold to the English, and put on trial at Rouen by a church court of clergy loyal to the English. The trial record survives, and it's astonishing.

For weeks, learned men question an unlettered nineteen-year-old, trying to trap her. The most well-known trap: do you know you are in God's grace? Say yes, and she's claiming a certainty no one can have.
Say no, and she's confessing guilt.

teach.h: IF I AM NOT, MAY GOD PUT ME THERE.
teach.b: She answers, in effect: if I am not, may God put me there; and if I am, may God keep me so. The court falls silent. They condemn her anyway.
On the thirtieth of May, 1431, she's burned in the marketplace at Rouen, asking for a cross to be held before her eyes, and calling on the name of Jesus.
Twenty-five years later a new church trial declared the verdict null: she'd been innocent. Too late. In 1920 the Catholic Church named her a saint.
What were her voices? People explain them many ways; the sources can't settle it.
She's often quoted as saying, I am not afraid; I was born to do this. Historians can't find that line in the records. But her answers at the trial show the same thing.

how: Joan of Arc is honored as a saint by the Catholic Church, with a feast day on May 30, and as a patron saint of France. Christians of many churches admire her courage and her answers at her trial.

games.q: you're Joan, nineteen, on trial. a judge asks: do you know you are in God's grace? yes sounds proud. no sounds guilty. what do you say?
o: if I am not, may God put me there; if I am, may God keep me so.
games.why: she slips the trap: if I am not, may God put me there; and if I am, may God keep me so. the record says her judges were stunned.

practice: Think of one true thing you've kept quiet because it's uncomfortable: you were wrong, something at work isn't fair, you need help, you love someone.
Notice where the fear sits in your body and breathe into it; you only need courage for one sentence, not a lifetime. If you pray, ask for it.
